title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money and Mutuality in the Thames

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, unhurried reading of Charles Dickens's last completed novel.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel about money — about what it does to people, what people will do for it, and what rare few will refuse it.
It's also a novel about the Thames — that dark, working river that carries bodies and secrets in equal measure.
To read it properly, you need more than one kind of eye.
Joining me today are three readers who bring three very different eyes to the page.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power.
He sees every institution in this novel — the law, philanthropy, the marriage market — as a mechanism for keeping people in their place.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes great fiction is finally about individual character — goodness, self-sacrifice, and the testing of the moral imagination.
He will tell us, with impeccable courtesy, when we are wrong.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who first read this novel as a teenager and has never quite left it.
She cares above all about the experience of reading — the sentences you stop and re-read, the characters who deserve better.
We begin today where the novel begins its deepest concerns: with money, and with what one family chooses to do without it.
What strikes me immediately about Our Mutual Friend is that Dickens understands money not as a backdrop but as the animating substance of every relationship in the book.
The Wilfer family scenes are where that understanding becomes most acute — and most moving — because here we watch characters actively choosing poverty over corruption.
R. Wilfer — the cherub, as Dickens calls him — delivers one of the most remarkable speeches in the novel when Bella comes back to him.
He has earned the right to say what he says, because he has been ground down by genteel poverty his entire life, and he knows what it costs.
Listen to what he tells Rokesmith about his daughter's choice.
'The mercenary young person distantly related to myself, did well! The mercenary young person distantly related to myself, did not trust to me in vain!'
'I admire this mercenary young person distantly related to myself, more in this dress than if she had come to me in China silks, Cashmere shawls, and Golconda diamonds.'
That triple repetition of 'mercenary young person distantly related to myself' — it's incantatory.
Wilfer is satirising the very language the novel's society uses to condemn Bella — and reclaiming it as a badge of honour.
Daniel is right that the speech is incantatory, though I would resist the word satirising.
What Wilfer is doing is something older and more fundamental than satire — he is pronouncing a blessing.
The ritual repetition is not ironic — it is liturgical.
And indeed the passage ends with the explicit invocation: 'My blessing on this engagement betwixt you.'
This is a father performing the one act of paternal authority that poverty has not stripped from him.
The scene that follows only deepens this.
The three of them sit down together to this simple supper, with the iron safe of Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles staring from the corner.
Dickens compares it — quite beautifully — to a fairy tale.

'It was, as Bella gaily said, like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, Somebody's been drinking my milk!'
'It was a delicious repast; by far the most delicious that Bella, or John Rokesmith, or even R. Wilfer had ever made.'
The fairy tale without the threat — without the territorial snarl — is happiness itself, for Dickens.
What I love about that passage is the 'gaily.'
Bella says it — she makes the comparison herself.
She has accepted poverty and she is not brave about it or stoic about it — she is gay about it.
That is a very precise thing for Dickens to give her.
And then there's that dragon in the corner — 'the two brass knobs of the iron safe staring like the eyes of some dull dragon.'
Veneering's commercial world is right there in the room with them, and they are entirely indifferent to it.
That's their freedom — not an escape from the world, but an achieved serenity within it.
Though I should say — the novel is not all supper parties and blessings.
There are figures in this book for whom there is no such serenity, and Dickens renders their suffering with terrible clarity.
Caroline is pointing at something essential.
The Wilfer supper is only legible as happiness against a backdrop of genuine despair elsewhere in the novel.
Bella's freedom to choose poverty is a freedom that Bradley Headstone, for instance, never had and never will have.
He clawed his way out of the working class through sheer discipline — and it has cost him everything human in him.
Dickens gives us a portrait of Bradley in extremity that is almost unbearable to read.
'Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face.'
'Its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating.'
He is being consumed from the inside — and Dickens is not sentimental about what produced him.
I would not disagree about Bradley — he is one of Dickens's most devastating creations.
But I think Daniel's framing — that Bradley is a product of the system, full stop — forecloses the moral question the novel is actually asking.
Bradley has agency.
He makes choices — terrible choices, driven by passion — and Dickens holds him to account for them.
The ashes spreading across his face are not capitalism — they are guilt, and they are earned.
And that tension — between the structural and the moral, between what the world does to us and what we do to ourselves — is going to be at the heart of everything we discuss today.
We're going to stay with that river, and those bodies, and those choices — moving deeper into what Dickens made of them.

segments.title: Bella's Reckoning: Love Against Mercenary Ambition

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart sentence by sentence and put it back together again.
Today's segment is called Bella's Reckoning: Love Against Mercenary Ambition.
We're asking a deceptively simple question: how does a young woman shaped by poverty and thwarted expectation learn to love without a price tag?
With me today are three readers who know this novel with unusual intimacy.

Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every institution in a novel as a machine for distributing power — and he's going to make sure we don't sentimentalise what Dickens is actually showing us.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes that great fiction is finally about individual moral character — tested, broken, and sometimes redeemed.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt is a critic who has re-read this novel more times than she'll admit, and who notices the things the rest of us miss on a first or second pass.
Let's begin with Bella herself — and with a passage that asks what she has actually grown up surrounded by.
What strikes me first about Bella's arc is how carefully Dickens anchors it in the world around her — not just her own vanity, but the degradation she witnesses.
There's a passage where Lizzie describes a child — a different girl, not Bella — but the portrait is doing work on the reader that I think bleeds into how we understand Bella's own formation.
Lizzie says, and I want to read this carefully:
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle—if she ever had one, Charley.'
That parenthesis — 'if she ever had one' — does something extraordinary.
In four words, Dickens strips the cradle of its sentimentality and makes it a privilege the poor can't assume.
And if you're reading Bella's story alongside this, you start to ask: what was her cradle?
Caroline's right that the passage is doing more than illustrating misery.
Notice that the child's father is described as 'a weak wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober' — and then immediately: 'But a good workman too, at the work he does.'
That qualification is devastating in its precision.
The system extracts his labour even as it destroys his person.
He is useful precisely to the degree that he is ruined.
Now set that beside John Harmon's predicament: a man whose father's entire fortune was a mechanism for evil, never for good.
Harmon himself puts it plainly — in his long interior reckoning he describes the trouble as stemming from
'the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence.'
The inheritance isn't a reward — it's a trauma handed down through property.
I want to resist the impulse to reduce all of this to economics, however.
What interests me in that interior monologue of Harmon's is the language of moral choice under impossible conditions.
He poses the question to himself with the clarity of a man who has genuinely examined his conscience.
He asks: 'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
That is not a political dilemma — it is a precisely observed moral dilemma.
And one, I'd argue, that only a man of genuine ethical seriousness could even formulate.
The novel's great achievement here is not to show us a system — it is to show us a person.
Edmund, I take the point — but I think Dickens insists that the person cannot be fully separated from the system.
What I find so remarkable in Harmon's self-examination is the phrase 'the girl so capriciously forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced.'
That doubled syntax — 'forced upon him,' 'forced upon whom he was forced' — enacts the mutuality of the trap.
Bella is not simply a test subject for John's scrutiny.
She is equally imprisoned by an arrangement she never consented to.
The verbal music of that passage is doing the argument for us, if we hear it.
And the novel is merciless in showing us what money does to supposedly disinterested institutions — not just individuals.
There's a comic set-piece where Boffin erupts about the proliferating titles attached to charitable giving.
Boffin says, and the list is crucial to the joke:

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
The escalating absurdity of those titles — including the Deceased — exposes how charity functions as a vanity market.
You buy prestige with five shillings and Dickens is furious about it.
The money that should redeem the poor is laundered through philanthropy into social capital for the rich.
The Boffin passage is genuinely funny, and I won't deny that.
But I'd note that Boffin's indignation is itself a moral response — the outrage of a good man at imposture.
Which brings me to Wegg — a character who is, in my view, among the most carefully observed studies in self-serving rationalisation in English fiction.
His scheme to extort Boffin is outlined with almost bureaucratic thoroughness.
He would have Boffin kept, in his own words,
'in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.'
The language of slavery used to describe a financial extortion is not accidental — but my point is that Wegg's wickedness is a wickedness of character, of a will utterly bent towards self.
The system does not make Wegg what he is — Wegg makes himself.
I'd push back gently on that.
Wegg's vocabulary is saturated with the logic of property and transaction.
He calls himself and Venus 'comrade, brother, and partner' — it's a parody of fraternal solidarity, but it's borrowed from commerce.
And note that he closes with the possibility that 'Halves' might be too modest — it might be more 'according to the rights of things' to say Two-thirds, or Three-fourths.
The language of rights has been colonised entirely by greed.
That is not personal wickedness alone — that is a man thinking in the categories his world has given him.
I keep coming back to Headstone in this context, actually — not because he's comic, but because he is where the novel's interest in torment without redemption becomes most unbearable.
There's a passage about what happens to a murderer who cannot feel remorse — and it's one of the strangest, most brilliant things Dickens ever wrote.
The narrator says:
'He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently.'
More efficiently.
That word is terrible — the obsessive mind not simply replaying the crime, but optimising it.
What Dickens has found here is a punishment more fitting than remorse, because it is wholly internal and wholly unforgiving.
That passage on Headstone is worth pausing over because it illuminates, by contrast, what genuine moral transformation looks like in the novel.
Headstone's tragedy is precisely the absence of the capacity for change.
He is, as the narrator puts it, 'a sullen unrepentant nature' — and the novel shows us that such a nature condemns itself more surely than any external verdict.
Bella's arc is the inverse of that — a nature that consents to being changed by love.
And that, I think, is what the novel finally asks us to value.
That distinction — the nature that refuses change against the nature that consents to it — feels like the very spine of this novel.
Headstone trapped in his eternal re-enactment, Bella learning to want something other than money — these are not separate stories.
They are two answers to the same question about what a self is capable of.
In our next segment, we'll follow the money further — into the dust-mounds and the wills and the whole elaborate machinery by which the novel asks who deserves to inherit.

segments.title: The Dust Heaps and Boffin's Soul: What Wealth Corrupts

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the programme that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — as seriously as it deserves.
I'm your host, and today we're drilling into one of the novel's great obsessions: what wealth does to people — and what it reveals about the society that produces it.
With me today are three readers who have thought long and hard about this book.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads novels as anatomies of class power — and who, I suspect, finds Our Mutual Friend almost disturbingly accurate.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don and lifelong Tory who believes the genius of great fiction lies in moral imagination, not social programme — and who will keep the rest of us honest.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has re-read this novel more times than she can count — and who notices things the rest of us walk straight past.
The dust heaps — those vast mounds of London refuse that underpin the Boffin fortune — are the novel's central image.
And today we want to follow the money: who asks for it, who uses it, and what it costs the soul.
The dust heaps are not just a colourful backdrop — they are the novel's thesis statement.
Boffin inherits wealth from the accumulated refuse of the city, and immediately becomes the target of every extractive institution in England.
Dickens catalogs this with savage precision in those letters the Secretary reads.
There is this magnificent sentence about the charities — let me read it:
"Oh the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold dust of the Golden Dustman!"
Dust for ocular use — that is, grit thrown in the eyes.
Every charity appeal is a form of blinding — keeping Boffin from seeing where the money actually goes.
Daniel will have his systems — and I don't dismiss them entirely.
But I think what Dickens is actually doing in those passages is something more immediately comic and more humanly precise than a structural critique.
He is anatomising hypocrisy — the wonderful, specific hypocrisy of people who dress greed in the language of benevolence.
Consider the Duke of Linseed's letter, which Dickens quotes in full — and the postscript in particular.
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
And then the P.S.: the Steward's fee is limited to three guineas.
The comedy lies in the collision between the ducal grandeur of the envelope and the petty commercial transaction within.
That is a joke about individual moral failure — about a duke who cannot see his own ridiculousness.
You're both right — but what moves me is how the comedy darkens when you reach the individual beggars in the very next passage.
The duke's letter is funny in a way that keeps you at a safe distance.
But then Dickens gives you the inspired beggars — sitting by a fragment of candle — and suddenly the comedy has real suffering inside it.
And then there is this line about their so-called documents, which I find devastating in its precision.
"They call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
Minced veal to a calf — it's grotesque and funny and slightly horrible all at once.
Dickens is mocking the beggars' pretensions — but the cruelty lands on a system that has reduced human beings to sending scraps of paper to a man they've never met.
Caroline puts her finger on something essential — the satire is never simply about the beggars' dishonesty.
It is about what the system produces: people so desperate they manufacture their own credentials out of nothing.
And there is a moment elsewhere in the novel where Dickens makes the logical endpoint of that desperation absolutely explicit.
It is the passage about Betty Higden by the river — one of the most extraordinary things in the book.
"Come to me, come to me! When the cruel shame and terror you have so long fled from, most beset you, come to me!"
"I am the Relieving Officer appointed by eternal ordinance to do my work; I am not held in estimation according as I shirk it."
"My breast is softer than the pauper-nurse's; death in my arms is peacefuller than among the pauper-wards."
The river speaks as a better Relieving Officer than the state — because the state's charity is so pitiless that death is the kinder relief.
That is not sentiment. That is an indictment.
I will not quarrel with the indictment — the Poor Law is a legitimate target and Dickens is devastating on it.
But I want to resist the reading that turns Boffin himself into merely a site of ideological contest.
The more interesting question is what wealth does to Boffin's character — to a genuinely good man placed in an impossible position.
And then there is this will that Wegg produces — the earlier will that would disinherit Boffin almost entirely.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
The old miser's voice is audible there — contemptuous, dismissive, and utterly blind to Boffin's worth.
What the novel explores is whether Boffin can remain himself despite the corruption that fortune — and Wegg — conspire to work upon him.
And Wegg himself is such a superb study in the way money warps those who don't even have it yet.
That scene where he mines away at an imaginary grindstone outside Boffin's keyhole — it's almost surreal.
"Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home."
The mime of power — grinding a man down without a word spoken.
And Boffin stooped at the keyhole — that image of the rich man bent down, peering out at his tormentor.
It reverses everything we expect from the dynamic of wealth and servility.
That reversal is precisely the point — Wegg has no money but he has leverage, and leverage is power.
The novel keeps showing us that wealth does not produce security — it produces new vulnerabilities.
Boffin is squeezed from above by dukes and earls with their circulars, from below by beggars with their scraps, and from the side by Wegg with his imaginary grindstone.
And then there is poor Sloppy — dressed in his new black suit by Mrs Boffin's kindness — and even that act of charity ends up as a kind of exposure.
Dickens writes that the tailor received directions to expend the utmost cunning of his art in concealing the buttons — and yet:
"he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators."
Sloppy's body refuses to be dressed up — refuses to pass as something it isn't.
The comedy is affectionate — but it also shows that class marks the body in ways that money cannot simply overwrite.
I find the Sloppy passage delightful rather than troubling — and I think that distinction matters.
Dickens is not mocking Sloppy's poverty — he is celebrating Sloppy's irrepressible particularity.
The buttons wink and gleam and tinkle — there is enormous vitality in that description.
Sloppy cannot be contained by tailoring science, as Dickens rather magnificently puts it — and that is to his credit, not his shame.
The novel's moral argument is not that money corrupts everything — it is that money corrupts those who have no other resource of character.
I think Edmund is right about Sloppy — the affection is genuine and the comedy is warm.
But I keep returning to Betty Higden, because she is the character the novel asks us to hold alongside all this comic satire.
The beggars writing to Boffin are faintly absurd — but Betty Higden is running from the same system those letters expose.
And the river calling to her — that image of death as the tenderer Relieving Officer — is not comic at all.
It is the novel saying: here is what happens when the satire runs out.
The satire runs out — and the novel asks us to feel the weight of what it has been describing all along.
The dust heaps, the charities, the beggars, the grindstone, the suit that won't stay shut — they all point to the same question: what does this society actually value?
We'll keep that question open as we move into our next segment.

segments.title: A Corpse Named Harmon: Disguise, Identity, and Victorian Plot

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been circling the Thames mud and the Veneering dinner table, but now we arrive at the novel's great structural gamble: John Harmon.
A man presumed dead, inheriting a fortune under a false name, watching his own life from the outside.
With me to pick this apart are three voices I trust enormously.
Dr. Daniel Rosen reads Dickens as a diagnostician of class power — and he will not let the plot's romantic surface go unexamined.
Sir Edmund Leigh brings a lifetime of reading novels as moral theatre — he will ask what this disguise costs the man wearing it.
And Ms. Caroline Woodcourt, who has read this book more times than she'll admit, will keep us honest about what it actually feels like on the page.
Let's begin with the Boffins — because before we can understand John Harmon the man, we need to understand what John Harmon the child endured.
What strikes me every time I return to Mr Boffin's account is the sheer physicality of it.
Dickens doesn't give us a generalised portrait of domestic cruelty — he gives us a bonnet.
A black straw bonnet, perched on top of Mrs Boffin's head as a matter of convenience, spinning across the yard.
And then Boffin's account of what follows — listen to how he tells it.
"I should have given him a rattler for himself, if Mrs Boffin hadn't thrown herself betwixt us, and received flush on the temple.
Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her."
That repetition — "Dropped her" — is everything.
It is grief dressed up as bluntness, because Boffin has no other language for feeling this large.
Caroline is quite right about the verbal texture, and I don't want to rush past it.
Boffin speaks in a dialect that the novel never condescends to — Dickens trusts its moral weight entirely.
What we are watching, of course, is the establishment of a surrogate family.
The Boffins are not John Harmon's parents, and they cannot protect him — but they refuse to stop trying.
And that refusal is the moral spine of the novel, long before the plot mechanics of disguise enter the frame.
One thinks of Burke — that the bonds of affection between persons who share a life are not contracts but something older and more binding.
Edmund's point about the surrogate family is well taken, but I want to push on what makes this scene so radical.
Old Harmon refuses to pay sixpence for the child's coach-money.
The fortune that will eventually purchase Bella Wilfer's redemption arc begins, here, as a miser's grip on a child's travel fare.
And look at what Mrs Boffin does in response — it is instinctive, bodily, class-blind.
"Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks."
That warmth — literal, physical warmth — is what the money cannot buy and what the system does not produce.
Dickens knows that the real inheritance John Harmon carries is not the dust mounds — it's that image of being held.
And Boffin actually tells us that Mrs Boffin never let it go — it stayed with her.
Years later, on cold nights, she would wake sobbing from the image of the boy's face.
And then there is this unbearable line she cries out — let me read it as Boffin gives it.
"I'd give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!"
The repetition of "wide wide" — that is a mother's voice, not a housekeeper's.
And it explains everything about why Mrs Boffin's later proposal — to adopt an orphan and name him John Harmon — is not sentiment.
It is grief finding a shape it can act upon.
That proposal of Mrs Boffin's is one of the most quietly astonishing moments in the novel.
She puts it with characteristic modesty — 'say it's only a whim' — and then says something of the deepest moral seriousness.
"Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him."
She proposes to make the name itself the vessel of care — to pour love into a name that has been robbed of its rightful owner.
This is, I think, Dickens's most serious meditation on what identity actually is.
Not the legal self, not the inherited name — but the love that was given, or withheld, in childhood.
Edmund frames that beautifully, and I want to bring it forward to what happens when the identity question is finally resolved — or rather, detonated.
John Harmon — now revealed as Rokesmith — confronts Wegg, and he is not gentle about it.
But what he says is not about the plot mechanics of disguise — it's about debt.
Moral debt — the only kind that actually matters in this novel.
"I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness — there are no words to satisfy me — of Mr and Mrs Boffin."
"There are no words to satisfy me" — that parenthesis is extraordinary.
Dickens is acknowledging that the language of the market — of property, of inheritance, of legal right — is simply insufficient for what the Boffins gave this child.
And there's a wonderful irony in that scene — Harmon is furious, and his fury is eloquent.
But his best argument against Wegg's mercenary presumption is precisely that he — Harmon — has renounced mercenary logic entirely.
And yet the whole disguise plot depended on him inhabiting a world of calculation and watchful concealment.
Which brings me to Dickens himself stepping forward in the postscript — because this is extraordinary, a novelist defending his own plot.
He says, with wonderful dry confidence, that he was not at pains to conceal the Harmon secret — he was at pains to suggest it.

"I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he."
It's almost teasing — he's saying, the joke is on the clever readers who thought they'd caught him out.
That postscript is one of the few moments in Victorian fiction where the author speaks in his own person to defend his art — and does so without a trace of apology.
He asks readers to grant the artist 'a little patience' — and that word, patience, carries enormous weight when applied to a serialised novel about a man who must wait to become himself.
Because that is finally what John Harmon is doing throughout the novel, isn't it?
He is waiting — as Mrs Boffin waited, as Boffin waited — for the moment when the name and the man can finally coincide.
I'd put it slightly differently: Harmon is waiting for the system to permit him to exist.
His father's will — that monstrous instrument — is the system in miniature: inheritance conditional on compliance with a stranger's preferences.
The disguise is not a plot convenience — it is the only rational response to a world that has decided, in advance, who you must be.
And what redeems the novel is that the Boffins — working people, people who smelled of the dust mounds — are the ones who finally set him free.
What a thread to pull — from a spinning bonnet in a yard, to a child's face frozen in Mrs Boffin's memory, to a man reclaiming his name in fury and gratitude.
In our next segment, we'll follow the dust mounds themselves — what they mean, who controls them, and why Dickens made a fortune out of rubbish.

segments.title: The Comic Surface: Dickens's Laughter in a Novel of Darkness

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the podcast that takes Dickens's last completed novel seriously — on every level, including its laughter.
Our Mutual Friend is a novel full of death, greed, and social corruption — and yet it is also extraordinarily funny.
Today we're asking: what is Dickens's comedy actually doing in a world this dark?
With me today are three guests who know this novel deeply and disagree about it productively.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads comic satire as a weapon — who gets skewered, and who benefits from the laughter.
Sir Edmund Leigh is a retired Oxford don who believes Dickens's humour is a moral gift — a way of seeing human beings whole.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has read this novel many times and can tell you exactly which passages make her laugh and which make her catch her breath.
Let's begin with the school scene — Dickens's portrait of charitable education, which is one of the most vicious comic set-pieces in all of English fiction.
What strikes me about the school scene is how precisely Dickens identifies the ideology at work beneath the comedy.
The humour is not gentle. It's an anatomy of a system that cannot see its own subjects as they actually are.
Young women hardened by poverty and exploitation are handed books about Little Margery — who, I should note, 'severely reproved and morally squashed the miller, when she was five and he was fifty.'
That detail — a five-year-old morally squashing a fifty-year-old man — is absurdist comedy, yes.
But it's also a precise description of how philanthropic literature constructs a fantasy working class — pious, grateful, and fundamentally childlike.
And Dickens names the logic explicitly: you were to do good, not because it was good, but because you were to make a good thing of it.
'You were to do good, not because it was good, but because you were to make a good thing of it.'
The moral education offered to the poor is, at its core, a training in self-interest dressed as virtue. The comedy exposes that — and it should make us uncomfortable.
Daniel is right about the satirical edge, though I think he underweights the sheer comic pleasure of the thing.
Dickens is not writing a pamphlet. He is writing a scene that is genuinely, riotously funny.
Consider the passage's final movement — the Sunday night classroom with its infant torments.

'The conventional boy smoothing away right and left, as an infallible commentary; the whole hot-bed of flushed and exhausted infants exchanging measles, rashes, whooping-cough, fever, and stomach disorders.'
That list — measles, rashes, whooping-cough, fever, stomach disorders — is Dickens at his most exuberant and most grotesque simultaneously.
One does not need to invoke ideology to recognise that this is a novelist at the height of his comic powers, observing the world with furious clarity.
The humour is moral precisely because it is human — it makes us feel the indignity suffered by those infants rather than merely arguing for it.
What I keep returning to is the rhythm of it. Dickens builds the chaos into the very sound of the prose.
There's that extraordinary sentence near the end of the description — listen to this:
'An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white, jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night.'
That repeated 'jumbled' — four times, then a fifth — it doesn't just describe disorder. It enacts it.
You feel your own mind beginning to lose its footing. Which is, of course, exactly what the school does to everyone inside it.
Caroline is touching on something important about technique — the form mirrors the content. But I want to press on what the comedy conceals as much as what it reveals.
Charley Hexam is being processed through this system. His sister Lizzie's sacrifice funds his education in this jumble.
And what comes out the other side? A young man who aspires to respectability by discarding everything and everyone that marks his origins.
The laughter at the school is devastating — but it doesn't save Charley. The system wins him in the end.
That's a sobering note — and it takes us naturally toward a very different kind of comedy in the novel.
The Boffin plot — the revelation that the Golden Dustman's miserly transformation was an elaborate performance — is one of the great comic surprises of Victorian fiction.
Caroline, you've described this as the passage you most wanted to read aloud. Let's hear it.
It is. Because the comedy here is inseparable from genuine tenderness — the two things are completely fused.
Bella has just placed her baby in John's arms — a lovely domestic detail — and then she kneels beside Mr Boffin.
And what she says to him is this:
'Please I have found out something not yet mentioned. Please I don't believe you are a hard-hearted miser at all, and please I don't believe you ever for one single minute were!'
That repeated 'please' — it's childlike, it's almost ceremonial. It has the quality of a prayer or a formal petition.
And Dickens gives us the laugh — 'an exultant ringing laugh' — at the same moment as the revelation and the reconciliation.
It's comic and it's moving and it's joyful all at once. I don't think any other Victorian novelist could quite manage that note.
I think Caroline is exactly right, and this is where I would gently part company with Daniel's framework.
The Boffin plot is not a satire of anything. It is a story about whether a person can change — and whether they can be forgiven when they recognise they were wrong.
Bella kneeling beside Boffin, drawing her arm over his shoulder — that is an image of moral restoration. And the comedy is its vehicle, not its disguise.
The novel rewards characters who earn their goodness. Bella does. And the laughter at this moment is the sound of relief — hers and ours.
I won't argue with the emotional power of that scene — it is genuinely affecting.
But I'd note that John Harmon's own account of his return to England is shot through with a very different kind of comedy — the comedy of a man who cannot trust himself.
He arrives already anxious that the money is corrupting him — that he is, in his own phrase, already growing avaricious.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That anaphora — 'shrinking... shrinking... mistrustful' — is almost comic in its compulsive self-examination. The man cannot stop cross-examining himself.
Which raises the question Bella's reunion with Boffin perhaps answers too neatly: can a person formed by a corrupting inheritance simply choose their way clear of it?
That question leads me to the Sloppy reveal — which is, I think, the novel's purest piece of theatrical comedy.
The scene is almost silent — and it has the timing of a great stage trick.
Wegg turns his head, and here is what he sees:
'Somebody else had come in quietly by the folding-doors. Turning his head, Wegg beheld his persecutor, the ever-wakeful dustman, accoutred with fantail hat and velveteen smalls complete.'
'Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's.'
'A face that was Sloppy's.' Full stop. Nothing more needed.
The comedy is entirely in the construction — in the gravity with which Dickens renders a man untying a fake broken head.
And Sloppy is significant — because he is one of those characters who exists almost entirely as a source of warmth and delight.
Daniel would say Sloppy is another victim of the system. I would say Dickens offers him to us as a rebuke to cynicism — a figure of uncomplicated goodness whose very name is a kind of comedy.
That Sloppy is the instrument of Wegg's unmasking is entirely fitting. The novel's lowest character defeats its most calculating villain.
There is a moral geometry to Dickens's comedy. Things resolve — not always tidily, but with a kind of rightness.
I'll accept the moral geometry — as long as we note that the geometry only works for some characters.
Sloppy's comedy is innocent and generous. Wegg's unmasking is satisfying. But the children in that school — the 'inclined plane of unfortunate infants' — they don't get a punchline that rescues them.
The laughter in this novel is distributed very unevenly — and that unevenness is itself a social fact that Dickens, perhaps half-consciously, has built into the architecture.
That feels like the crux of it — whether Dickens's comedy is a great leveller, or whether it reveals the very inequalities it appears to dissolve.
We've moved from the grotesque schoolroom to Bella's kneeling reconciliation to a man untying a fake broken head — and somehow all of it feels like the same novelist.
That range — from the savage to the tender to the farcical — is perhaps the most distinctive thing about Our Mutual Friend's comic voice.
We'll continue with another dimension of this extraordinary novel after the break.

segments.title: Transformation and Redemption: Reading Mutual Friendship

utterances.text: We've arrived at the closing passage of our conversation today — and it feels right to end where Dickens himself so often ends: with questions of identity, disguise, and what it means to truly know another person.
We have four passages in front of us that pull in quite different directions — tenderness, accusation, betrayal, and a young man in a sailor's disguise trying to see his future wife plain.
Edmund, I'd like to start with you — because you've been our guide to the novel's moral imagination, and two of these passages sit at very different ends of that moral spectrum.
Thank you. Let me begin with what I consider the most quietly devastating moment in this entire section.
It is the Boffins — that dear, ungainly, magnificent pair — sitting side by side and being pronounced, by Dickens's narrator, a hopelessly Unfashionable couple.
Dickens capitalises the word. Unfashionable. As though it were a title of honour — which, of course, it is.
Mr Boffin speaks to his wife, and the line is this:
"Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!"
There is no wit in that line. No epigram. No irony. And that is precisely its power.
Dickens understood — as Burke understood — that the deepest affections are also the most inarticulate. They do not reach for decoration.
And the satirical sting — that their goodness ruins their social aspirations — that is Dickens at his most precise. Virtue is incompatible with fashionability. He means it absolutely.
What moves me about that passage is the word "pleasant." He reaches for it twice.
It's not a grand word. It's almost modest. But in Mr Boffin's mouth it carries a whole lifetime.
"This many and many a year" — that rhythm. I find it genuinely moving every time I read it.
And then Dickens delivers his verdict — "a hopelessly Unfashionable pair" — with that extraordinary capital U — and somehow it's both comic and a benediction.
I don't want to drain the tenderness from that passage — it is tender, genuinely so — but I think we need to sit with what Dickens is actually saying about the social world these two inhabit.
The Boffins are good people who have come into money. And Dickens's verdict is that their goodness makes them socially impossible.
That is a structural observation, not a sentimental one. The fashion system — the class system — is built to exclude precisely this kind of human warmth.
So yes, it's a benediction — but it's also an indictment. Dickens gives them his love and condemns the world that has no room for them in the same breath.
Daniel, I won't quarrel with that — but I'd resist the word structural, because it flattens something important.
The novel's satirical energy isn't simply aimed at a system. It's aimed at pretension — at individuals who choose vanity over decency.
The Boffins' ruin is comic precisely because it is also a moral triumph. Dickens doesn't mourn for them — he congratulates them.
Now — the Riderhood passages are a rather different matter, and I confess they trouble me far more.
Let's go there. Because Roger Riderhood is one of the novel's great study in self-serving testimony — and his accusation against Gaffer Hexam is a masterclass in moral ugliness dressed as civic duty.
Edmund, you have both of those passages. What do you make of Dickens's ventriloquism here?
Riderhood is, I think, one of Dickens's least celebrated triumphs. He is irredeemably corrupt — and yet every word he speaks has its own appalling internal logic.
Listen to how he makes his formal accusation. The syntax itself performs respectability:
"I give information that the man that done the Harmon Murder is Gaffer Hexam, the man that found the body."
And then — "His hand and no other." Four words. Like a courtroom stamp.
But then comes the second passage — and here Dickens does something extraordinary. He lets Riderhood quote Gaffer quoting himself.
The reported confession — allegedly Gaffer's own words — runs like this:
"There was foul play then. I done it for his money. Don't betray me!"
And Riderhood adds — with his characteristic precision about unreliability — "Those were the words as ever he used."
It's beautifully vile. The protestation of accuracy from the least trustworthy man in the novel.
Edmund has put his finger on something essential — and I want to push it a step further.
Riderhood invokes what he calls "the obligations of a Alfred David" — his mangled version of "affidavit" — as a guarantee of truthfulness.
He is performing legal legitimacy for an audience — Lightwood, the police — who represent institutional power.
And the institutions accept his performance. That is Dickens's point about law in this novel — it cannot tell a performed truth from a real one.
The man who did not commit the murder is named by the law. The man doing the naming walks free. That is not a quirk of plot — that is a system working exactly as designed.
What strikes me reading both Riderhood passages together is the sheer verbal texture of the man. He's horrible — but he's also one of the most alive voices in the novel.
"Rogue Riderhood" — Gaffer calls him that even inside Riderhood's own retelling. It's almost comic that he reports the insult so faithfully.
And yet the passage has genuine menace. "He falls a shaking." That repetition — "a shaking worse" the second time — it has the rhythm of a nightmare.
Dickens lets the ugliness be vivid and almost funny at once. That unsettles you more than pure horror would.
And then we arrive at John Harmon — or whoever he is at this moment in the novel — and a very different kind of deception.
The sailor's disguise, the careful observation of Bella Wilfer, the desire to see someone true before being seen yourself.
Caroline — this is very much in your territory. What is Dickens doing with this kind of identity play?
What I love about this passage is how Harmon describes the plot almost with embarrassment — as though he can hear how it sounds.
He and Radfoot devise this scheme, and the language Harmon uses for it is almost self-deprecating. He calls it simply "the plot":
"the plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way"
"Trying to put ourselves in her way" — there's something almost boyish about that phrasing. This is a man of wealth and inheritance reduced to hoping for a chance encounter.
And what he wants is simply to see her plain — unguarded, unperforming. That is a deeply sympathetic desire. It's also, of course, a form of surveillance.
Caroline names it perfectly — surveillance. And I think we should be honest about what power dynamic is operating here.
John Harmon has the freedom to disguise himself, to test Bella, to observe her without her consent. Bella has none of that freedom.
She is being evaluated. Her character is under examination by a man who holds, quite literally, her financial future.
The novel frames this as romantic. And there is genuine tenderness in Harmon's account. But the structure underneath it is that of property inspecting its acquisition.
I think Daniel is identifying something real — but I'd push back on the framing. Harmon is not a predator. He is a man trying to escape the predatory logic of the will that haunts him.
He observes Bella precisely because he refuses to marry her as a transaction — as the will demands. The disguise is, in that sense, an act of respect.
He even checks his own account of the facts at the end of the passage — "I have all these facts right? Yes. They are all accurately right." The self-interrogation of a scrupulous conscience.
Contrast that with Riderhood — who also claims accuracy, also protests his fidelity to fact. The difference is everything.

That connection Edmund has just made — between Riderhood's "those were the words as ever he used" and Harmon's "they are all accurately right" — that is the kind of thing that makes you love this novel.
Two men claiming the accuracy of their testimony. One of them lying to destroy a man. One of them telling the truth to free himself.
Dickens is asking us to read the difference — to develop that moral ear. That is what the whole novel trains us to do.
And on that note — the moral ear, the trained reader, the novel as instrument of discernment — I think we've found the right place to close.

We've moved today from the Boffins' quiet dignity to Riderhood's performed certainty to Harmon's careful anonymity — and in each case the novel has asked us the same question: who is trustworthy, and how do you know?
My thanks to Edmund Leigh, Daniel Rosen, and Caroline Woodcourt — three readers who bring real intelligence and real feeling to this magnificent, strange, inexhaustible book.
Thank you for listening to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked. We'll be back with another episode soon.

c49:p74.text:
‘And therefore—and therefore,’ the cherub went on in a glowing
      voice, as Bella’s hand stole gradually up his waistcoat to his neck, ‘this
      mercenary young person distantly related to myself, refused the price,
      took off the splendid fashions that were part of it, put on the
      comparatively poor dress that I had last given her, and trusting to my
      supporting her in what was right, came straight to me. Have I led up to
      it?’
c49:p74.summary: R. Wilfer blesses the engagement, declaring his profound admiration for Bella's choice to accept poverty with Rokesmith rather than wealth, and affirming that her choice is the truest fortune.
c49:p74.best_quote: The mercenary young person distantly related to myself, did well! The mercenary young person distantly related to myself, did not trust to me in vain! I admire this mercenary young person distantly related to myself, more in this dress than if she had come to me in China silks, Cashmere shawls, and Golconda diamonds. I love this young person dearly. I say to the man of this young person's heart, out of my heart and with all of it, "My blessing on this engagement betwixt you, and she brings you a good fortune when she brings you the poverty she has accepted for your sake and the honest truth's!"

c65:p104.text:
Not one other word did Bradley utter all that night. Not once did he
      change his attitude, or loosen his hold upon his wrist. Rigid before the
      fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with

      haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being

      degenerating.

c18:p149.text:
‘The child’s father is employed by the house that employs me; that’s how I
      came to know it, Charley. The father is like his own father, a weak
      wretched trembling creature, falling to pieces, never sober. But a good
      workman too, at the work he does. The mother is dead. This poor ailing
      little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people
      from her cradle—if she ever had one, Charley.’
c18:p149.summary: Lizzie explains that Bella's father is employed by her employer and shares his father's weakness for drink; her mother is dead, and the child is surrounded by alcoholics and degradation.

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.
c31:p1.best_quote: When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.

c31:p109.text:
‘I don’t. And if  they  do, my dear, they ought to learn better,’ said Mr
      Boffin. ‘Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses,
      and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and
      Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities
      that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among ’em pretty well up to
      his neck! If Mr Tom Noakes gives his five shillings ain’t he a Patron, and
      if Mrs Jack Styles gives her five shillings ain’t she a Patroness? What
      the deuce is it all about? If it ain’t stark staring impudence, what do
      you call it?’
c31:p109.summary: Mr Boffin delivers a scathing critique of the proliferation of patronage titles and the pretension of charity donors who expect public recognition for their contributions.
c31:p109.best_quote: Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!

c40:p72.text:
On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.
c40:p72.summary: Wegg proposes an elaborate scheme: let Boffin excavate the Mounds at his own expense while they observe, then when the work is done, threaten him with the earlier will and extort half his property. If Boffin is caught secretly removing anything, they will interrogate and enslave him morally until he pays for his freedom.
c40:p72.best_quote: That, he considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, 'Halves!' ... he should be kept in a state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.

c57:p53.text:
Now, too, was he cursed with a state of mind more wearing and more
      wearisome than remorse. He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold
      that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing
      the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently. In the defensive
      declarations and pretended confessions of murderers, the pursuing shadow
      of this torture may be traced through every lie they tell. If I had done
      it as alleged, is it conceivable that I would have made this and this
      mistake? If I had done it as alleged, should I have left that unguarded
      place which that false and wicked witness against me so infamously deposed
      to? The state of that wretch who continually finds the weak spots in his
      own crime, and strives to strengthen them when it is unchangeable, is a
      state that aggravates the offence by doing the deed a thousand times
      instead of once; but it is a state, too, that tauntingly visits the
      offence upon a sullen unrepentant nature with its heaviest punishment
      every time.
c57:p53.summary: The narrator explores the psychological torment of murderers without remorse: they are compelled to endlessly re-enact and mentally perfect their crime, creating a torture worse than remorse itself.
c57:p53.best_quote: He had no remorse; but the evildoer who can hold that avenger at bay, cannot escape the slower torture of incessantly doing the evil deed again and doing it more efficiently.

c17:p4.text:
But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.
c17:p4.summary: The Secretary describes the flood of charitable solicitations and scheme proposals that inundate the Boffins, including a satirical example of a duke's letter requesting Boffin become a Steward of a charity for a three-guinea fee.
c17:p4.best_quote: Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?

In those pleasant little towns on Thames, you may hear the fall of the
      water over the weirs, or even, in still weather, the rustle of the rushes;
      and from the bridge you may see the young river, dimpled like a young
      child, playfully gliding away among the trees, unpolluted by the
      defilements that lie in wait for it on its course, and as yet out of
      hearing of the deep summons of the sea. It were too much to pretend that
      Betty Higden made out such thoughts; no; but she heard the tender river
      whispering to many like herself, ‘Come to me, come to me! When the cruel
      shame and terror you have so long fled from, most beset you, come to me! I
      am the Relieving Officer appointed by eternal ordinance to do my work; I
      am not held in estimation according as I shirk it. My breast is softer
      than the pauper-nurse’s; death in my arms is peacefuller than among the
      pauper-wards. Come to me!’

      hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators. The
      artistic taste of some unknown hatter had furnished him with a hatband of
      wholesale capacity which was fluted behind, from the crown of his hat to
      the brim, and terminated in a black bunch, from which the imagination
      shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted. Some special powers with which
      his legs were endowed, had already hitched up his glossy trousers at the
      ankles, and bagged them at the knees; while similar gifts in his arms had
      raised his coat-sleeves from his wrists and accumulated them at his
      elbows. Thus set forth, with the additional embellishments of a very
      little tail to his coat, and a yawning gulf at his waistband, Sloppy stood

‘The last time me and Mrs Boffin saw the poor boy,’ said Mr Boffin,
      warming (as fat usually does) with a tendency to melt, ‘he was a child of
      seven year old. For when he came back to make intercession for his sister,
      me and Mrs Boffin were away overlooking a country contract which was to be
      sifted before carted, and he was come and gone in a single hour. I say he
      was a child of seven year old. He was going away, all alone and forlorn,
      to that foreign school, and he come into our place, situate up the yard of
      the present Bower, to have a warm at our fire. There was his little scanty
      travelling clothes upon him. There was his little scanty box outside in
      the shivering wind, which I was going to carry for him down to the
      steamboat, as the old man wouldn’t hear of allowing a sixpence
      coach-money. Mrs Boffin, then quite a young woman and pictur of a
      full-blown rose, stands him by her, kneels down at the fire, warms her two
      open hands, and falls to rubbing his cheeks; but seeing the tears come
      into the child’s eyes, the tears come fast into her own, and she holds him
      round the neck, like as if she was protecting him, and cries to me, “I’d
      give the wide wide world, I would, to run away with him!” I don’t say but
      what it cut me, and but what it at the same time heightened my feelings of
      admiration for Mrs Boffin. The poor child clings to her for awhile, as she
      clings to him, and then, when the old man calls, he says “I must go! God
      bless you!” and for a moment rests his heart against her bosom, and looks
      up at both of us, as if it was in pain—in agony. Such a look! I went
      aboard with him (I gave him first what little treat I thought he’d like),
      and I left him when he had fallen asleep in his berth, and I came back to
      Mrs Boffin. But tell her what I would of how I had left him, it all went
      for nothing, for, according to her thoughts, he never changed that look
      that he had looked up at us two. But it did one piece of good. Mrs Boffin
      and me had no child of our own, and had sometimes wished that how we had
      one. But not now. “We might both of us die,” says Mrs Boffin, “and other
      eyes might see that lonely look in our child.” So of a night, when it was
      very cold, or when the wind roared, or the rain dripped heavy, she would
      wake sobbing, and call out in a fluster, “Don’t you see the poor child’s
      face? O shelter the poor child!”—till in course of years it gently
      wore out, as many things do.’

      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John

c18:p1.text:
It was a school for all ages, and for both sexes. The latter were kept
      apart, and the former were partitioned off into square assortments. But,
      all the place was pervaded by a grimly ludicrous pretence that every pupil
      was childish and innocent. This pretence, much favoured by the
      lady-visitors, led to the ghastliest absurdities. Young women old in the
      vices of the commonest and worst life, were expected to profess themselves
      enthralled by the good child’s book, the Adventures of Little Margery, who
      resided in the village cottage by the mill; severely reproved and morally
      squashed the miller, when she was five and he was fifty; divided her
      porridge with singing birds; denied herself a new nankeen bonnet, on the
      ground that the turnips did not wear nankeen bonnets, neither did the
      sheep who ate them; who plaited straw and delivered the dreariest orations
      to all comers, at all sorts of unseasonable times. So, unwieldy young
      dredgers and hulking mudlarks were referred to the experiences of Thomas
      Twopence, who, having resolved not to rob (under circumstances of uncommon
      atrocity) his particular friend and benefactor, of eighteenpence,
      presently came into supernatural possession of three and sixpence, and
      lived a shining light ever afterwards. (Note, that the benefactor came to
      no good.) Several swaggering sinners had written their own biographies in
      the same strain; it always appearing from the lessons of those very
      boastful persons, that you were to do good, not because it  was  good, but
      because you were to make a good thing of it. Contrariwise, the adult
      pupils were taught to read (if they could learn) out of the New Testament;
      and by dint of stumbling over the syllables and keeping their bewildered
      eyes on the particular syllables coming round to their turn, were as
      absolutely ignorant of the sublime history, as if they had never seen or
      heard of it. An exceedingly and confoundingly perplexing jumble of a
      school, in fact, where black spirits and grey, red spirits and white,
      jumbled jumbled jumbled jumbled, jumbled every night. And particularly
      every Sunday night. For then, an inclined plane of unfortunate infants
      would be handed over to the prosiest and worst of all the teachers with
      good intentions, whom nobody older would endure. Who, taking his stand on
      the floor before them as chief executioner, would be attended by a
      conventional volunteer boy as executioner’s assistant. When and where it
      first became the conventional system that a weary or inattentive infant in
      a class must have its face smoothed downward with a hot hand, or when and
      where the conventional volunteer boy first beheld such system in
      operation, and became inflamed with a sacred zeal to administer it,
      matters not. It was the function of the chief executioner to hold forth,
      and it was the function of the acolyte to dart at sleeping infants,
      yawning infants, restless infants, whimpering infants, and smooth their
      wretched faces; sometimes with one hand, as if he were anointing them for
      a whisker; sometimes with both hands, applied after the fashion of
      blinkers. And so the jumble would be in action in this department for a
      mortal hour; the exponent drawling on to My Dearert Childerrenerr, let us
      say, for example, about the beautiful coming to the Sepulchre; and
      repeating the word Sepulchre (commonly used among infants) five hundred
      times, and never once hinting what it meant; the conventional boy
      smoothing away right and left, as an infallible commentary; the whole
      hot-bed of flushed and exhausted infants exchanging measles, rashes,
      whooping-cough, fever, and stomach disorders, as if they were assembled in
      High Market for the purpose.
